analysis.one_liner: Requires OSHA to write a federal safety standard on workplace violence, including shootings.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the House Education and Labor Committee from April 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023, never receiving a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would direct the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health to study how to reduce violence at work, including gun violence, and require the Labor Department's workplace safety agency (OSHA) to turn that research into an enforceable safety standard within four years. Today there is no federal standard that specifically requires employers to take steps to prevent violence on the job. The bill was introduced in April 2022, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, and never moved again before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in jobs with high exposure to violence — retail clerks, health care and social service workers, delivery drivers, and teachers — would gain enforceable protections if the standard required violence-prevention plans, training, or security measures. Unions and worker safety groups would also gain a new enforcement tool.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in violence-prone jobs like retail and health care

how_it_helps.text: Directs NIOSH to study ways to reduce the threat of workplace violence, including firearm violence, and submit recommendations within 15 months.
Requires OSHA to issue a binding occupational safety and health standard on reducing workplace violence within four years of enactment, considering the NIOSH recommendations.
Currently, OSHA's general duty duty clause covers violence only indirectly; this would create a specific, enforceable standard employers must follow.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially retailers, hospitals, clinics, and service businesses — would bear the cost of complying with a new violence-prevention standard: written prevention programs, training, staffing or security measures, and recordkeeping. Some costs could be passed to consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers in retail, health care, and services

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on businesses, and small businesses with thin margins could face disproportionate burdens from prevention plans, training, and security requirements.
The standard allows up to four years after enactment to be issued, and rulemaking often takes longer, so protections would arrive slowly even if the bill became law.

A workplace-violence standard addresses how employers respond to violence, not the availability of firearms itself, so it would not directly change the underlying risk of gun violence; critics of this approach argue it treats symptoms rather than causes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers in the highest-risk occupations, a specific enforceable standard could prevent injuries and deaths, and the compliance costs to employers are real but comparable to those of any safety rule OSHA already issues. The main design weakness is timing: a four-year runway plus normal rulemaking means protections could take five or more years, and the study-first structure adds delay. It is a meaningful but slow-moving benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee when introduced and never received any committee action, hearing, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Safe Workplaces Act was introduced on April 18, 2022 by Rep. Joe Neguse with 20 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No further action was taken — no markup, hearing, or vote — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced the cost of a new OSHA violence-prevention standard are better off because the bill never advanced. Workers in high-risk jobs remain without a federal workplace-violence standard.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoiding new safety compliance costs

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing OSHA to issue a workplace-violence safety standard.

for.name: 20 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of jurisdiction, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, so it never advanced past referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats and the Republican-controlled committee of jurisdiction took no action; the record shows no Republican support.

industries.industry: Employers in retail, health care, and other service sectors
industries.note: A specific OSHA standard on workplace violence would impose compliance costs — prevention plans, training, and security measures — on employers, whose interest in avoiding those costs runs against workers' interest in protection. The bill's failure leaves these employers free of new requirements.

The bill counts firearm violence as a workplace hazard, so a standard could affect how gun retailers and other workplaces manage firearm-related threats, though the bill regulates workplace safety practices rather than gun sales directly.

industries.industry: Occupational safety and health services (training, consulting, security)
industries.note: Firms providing safety training, violence-prevention consulting, and workplace security would gain customers if employers had to implement prevention programs.
